name: Esther Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at the Prairie Deep potash mine, about a kilometre underground. A continuous miner is a long machine with a spinning cutting head that chews through the potash and loads it onto a conveyor, so there's no blasting. I start at seven, check the cutting plan, and then it's hours of steering a machine the size of a bus through rooms we cut in a grid. For the last year I've also been one of two operators testing the remote-guided version from a control room near the shaft. I love problem-solving underground, and I hate the drive to the mine in winter whiteouts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up testing the remote version?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I volunteered. I've always been the one who reads the manual first, and these days I use an AI assistant every day, for planning cuts, for checking fault codes, even for learning Spanish on the drive home. My husband Samuel teaches high school science, and our twins are grown, Ruth is an accountant and David is in the navy. Samuel says I treat every new gadget like a puzzle box. He's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a useful helper, not a revolution, and I'd keep using it. It makes my shift reports faster and helps me catch problems early. I'd post something like that if anyone asked, but I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job until I decide to stop, probably at sixty-two or sixty-three. I'd be a little bored, to be truthful, because I like when things change. But financially it's the safe picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the continuous miner and keep testing the remote unit when they ask. I'd keep using AI for everything it's good at and maybe help the training department write better guides. Samuel and I would keep our usual savings, about five hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little restlessness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bored. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find something new to learn. Maybe I'd finally do the online course in industrial controls I keep putting off. I'm the type who has to be moving or I get grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Potash prices, the same as always. When fertilizer prices drop, the mine slows down and cuts overtime. That's real and it has nothing to do with computers.

S0.say: AI is a useful helper, not a revolution, and I'd keep using it. It makes my shift reports faster and helps me catch problems early.
S0.think: My job stays my job until I decide to stop, probably at sixty-two or sixty-three. I'd be a little bored, but financially it's the safe picture.
S0.do: Keeps running the continuous miner and testing the remote unit. Keeps using AI daily, helps the training department write guides and saves about five hundred a month.
S0.quote: I'm the type who has to be moving or I get grumpy.
S0.fieldNote: Esther is the curious one who volunteered for the remote trial, and the plateau mostly bores her. She keeps her public views measured and practical. Her long-standing worry is commodity prices, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming whether we like it or not, so people should get ahead of it. The company should train people and the government should help those who struggle. I'd also say it's not all bad, because the dangerous parts of mining are the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm already one of two people who can run the remote miner. If the whole mine goes that way, someone has to lead the control room, and I'd like it to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for any control room lead role the moment it's posted, probably in the first year. I'd take that controls course and use AI to study for it in the evenings. I'd also push the company to bring the older operators along, because they know the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle most on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dale, who's been here thirty-five years and still writes his notes in a little book. He's the best at feeling bad ground, but he'd hate the screens. I'd want him beside me in the control room for that reason, not pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd overreach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, I might apply for a role and lose it to a young engineer. That's fine. I'd rather try and miss than sit still and get moved.

S1.say: Change is coming, so people should get ahead of it, with training from the company and help from government for those who struggle. The dangerous parts of mining go first, which isn't all bad.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, since I'm one of two people who can run the remote miner. If the whole mine goes that way, someone has to lead the control room, and I'd like it to be me.
S1.do: Applies for a control room lead role as soon as it's posted in the first year. Takes an industrial controls course with AI as a study aid and pushes the company to bring older operators along.
S1.quote: I'd rather try and miss than sit still and get moved.
S1.fieldNote: Esther sees steady change as an opening and plans to move first. She is confident but realistic that a younger engineer might beat her to a role. Her respect for older colleagues like Dale shows she values ground knowledge, not just screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle well, and we need emergency help for workers and towns, quickly. I'd also say people should stop pretending it isn't happening. Online I'd probably share practical guides on what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with new tech only buys me a year or two. If AI can run the whole mine, the control room needs one person, not twenty, and maybe nobody. At sixty, with about five months saved, I'd be out of mining for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent package and leave on my terms rather than wait. Then I'd offer myself as a short-term adviser to other mines switching over, because I've actually run one of these machines. Samuel and I would cut the second car and hold our savings for the gap until his pension and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have moves, but I'd be making them fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave before being pushed. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very, but the first package is usually the best one. I've seen it with the potash downturn in 2016, the people who went first got eighteen months' pay. The people who waited got six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Samuel's teaching job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. If AI can teach chemistry, maybe they'd keep teachers for the human side, or maybe not. That's the scary part, we might both be in the same boat.

S2.say: This is too fast for anyone to handle well, and workers and towns need emergency help quickly. People should stop pretending it isn't happening.
S2.think: Being good with tech only buys me a year or two, because a fully AI-run mine needs one person in the control room, maybe nobody. At sixty, with about five months saved, I'd be out of mining for good.
S2.do: Takes the first decent package and leaves on her own terms. Offers herself as a short-term adviser to mines switching over, sells the second car and holds savings for the gap to pension.
S2.feel: Anxious, with moves left but having to make them fast.
S2.quote: I've seen it with the potash downturn in 2016, the people who went first got eighteen months' pay. The people who waited got six.
S2.fieldNote: Esther recognises that even early adopters lose out when the end point arrives this soon. Her instinct is to move first and take the best package, based on what she saw in a past downturn. The uncertainty about her husband's teaching job is her hidden worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's be smart about it: retrain, plan and don't panic. Companies should share timelines and governments should fund training. I'd say that at work and in our community group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to land well. I'd lead the control room for a few years, build a name, and be at sixty-three by the time it's all automated. Then I could retire or advise, depending on the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the control room lead job in year one and build up savings from five months to a year. I'd set up a small consulting business on the side, just to see if other mines would pay for my experience. I'd also put a little into a robotics fund, because if robots are taking the jobs, I'd like a slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in robotics. Isn't that betting against your own crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it feels that way. But it's not like my not buying it would stop the robots. If it pays off, I can help my kids, which is the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does 2031 feel compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'm sprinting. In 2031 I'm jogging with a map. I can make choices instead of just reacting.

S3.say: We have five years, so let's be smart: retrain, plan and don't panic. Companies should share timelines and governments should fund training.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to land well. I'd lead the control room for a few years, build a name, and be sixty-three when it's all automated, then retire or advise.
S3.do: Goes for the control room lead job in year one and builds savings from five months toward a year. Starts a small consulting business on the side and puts a little into a robotics fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more interested than worried.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'm sprinting. In 2031 I'm jogging with a map.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Esther's adaptability becomes an advantage again. She plans across several fronts at once: job, side business and investments. She is unapologetic about investing in the robots, which she sees as protecting her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and nobody should waste it. Everyone in mining should be learning something new by next year. I'd probably start a group chat for people at the mine who want to share what they're learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good picture. I'd lead the control room, help commission the new systems and retire at sixty-three or sixty-four, before it all finishes. I'd probably enjoy the last years more than any before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the miner and keep testing the remote systems until they go mine-wide. I'd invest a little each month in a broad fund that includes robotics and AI companies. And I'd keep using AI tools every day, so I'm always the one who knows how they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any part of this picture bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town, a bit. Prairie Deep employs about eight hundred people, and the school and hockey rink depend on them. I'd want the company and the government to have a plan for the town after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth and David?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's an accountant, which is right in the firing line, so I'd tell her to start moving toward advising people, the human part. David in the navy, I honestly don't know. I'd tell them both to save more than we did.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, and nobody should waste it. Everyone in mining should be learning something new by next year.
S4.think: For me it's a good picture. I'd lead the control room, help commission the new systems and retire at sixty-three or sixty-four before it all finishes.
S4.do: Keeps running the miner and testing remote systems until they go mine-wide. Invests a little each month in a broad fund including robotics and AI companies and keeps using AI tools daily.
S4.quote: Prairie Deep employs about eight hundred people, and the school and hockey rink depend on them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Esther expects her last working years to be her most interesting. Her worry moves outward to the town and to her daughter's exposed accounting career. She keeps an even, pragmatic tone and favours shared responsibility between company and government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time for being adaptable to pay off. What would help is a fair exit package and a bridge to the pension for people over fifty-five, plus some honest timelines from the companies so we can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd miss it. I would. There's a moment when the cutting head bites into fresh potash and the whole room smells like salt and wet rock, and I've never found that anywhere else.

headlineQuote: There's a moment when the cutting head bites into fresh potash and the whole room smells like salt and wet rock, and I've never found that anywhere else.
portrait: Esther Ibrahim is a 58-year-old continuous miner operator at an underground potash mine who volunteered to test the remote-guided version and uses AI every day. She is pragmatic and centre in her views, and she likes to move first. The plateau mostly bores her and steady change excites her, since she hopes to lead the control room. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because her adaptability would only buy a year or two, but with five or ten years she plans a side business, invests and expects to retire on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for her adaptability to pay off.
whatWouldHelp: A fair exit package and a bridge to the pension for workers over fifty-five, plus honest timelines from companies.
